newsitem.title: MONACO: OLYMPICS-IOC ACCUSED OF INEFFICIENT DRUG TESTING IN ATLANTA.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC ACCUSED OF INEFFICIENT DRUG TESTING IN ATLANTA.

text.p: An international sports official on Thursday accused Olympic chiefs of worrying more about the image of the Games than running an efficient drug-testing operation to catch cheats at last year's Atlanta Olympics.

The official, who did not want to be identified, said the organisation of the Atlanta laboratory left a lot to be desired and the results of a new machine, hailed as a revolutionary way of catching drug offenders before the Games, were not used at all to nail cheats.
"I get the impression they were more concerned about their image," the official told Reuters. "There were problems with the training of the people in the lab."
Before the Olympics, officials paraded the high-resolution mass spectrometer as a major step forward because it is able to trace banned substances in the body back over a longer period.
But last November the IOC admitted it had not been satisfied with the reliability of the testing procedures on the machine and a handful of positive urine samples had been rejected.

Olympic sources revealed this week that the IOC ultimately decided against using any of the results from the machine. In private, many experienced officials have been critical of the way the whole drug-testing was run in Atlanta.
"The whole thing won't be run like that again," one Olympic source said. "None of the results of the spectrometer were used."
The result was that the Olympic Games, the most prestigious sporting event in the world, did not have the toughest drug-testing available.

Many experts were surprised in Atlanta that only two athletes were caught taking steroids. The testing is regarded as being unfair because there are presently athletes in the world who have been banned after their tests were analysed by the spectrometer at other events.

Australian sprinter Dean Capobianco, for example, is fighting a four-year ban for steroids on the grounds that two drug tests he gave during a short period last year produced different results -- one positive, one negative.
The positive result came from a test which was analysed on the spectrometer while the negative test was not analysed by the machine.
The overall organisation in Atlanta has come under heavy fire from the media.

U.S. officials only recently sent the key documents -- including drug test results -- to athletics's governing body following the world records of Canadian sprinter Donovan Bailey and Michael Johnson in the Atlanta men's 100 and 200 metres respectively.
Proof of a negative drug result must be provided by organisers before any world record can be ratified. The documents must usually be supplied to athletics authorities within one month.

On Wednesday Carl Lewis accused American athletics chiefs of trying to hush up the abuse of performance-enhancing drugs in U.S. sport after it was revealed that two more American athletes had been caught doping outside the Games.
